# C6. The cross-country test {#esc-oecd26}

Section {{< var p.sec_esc_crossSection >}} of the paper tests the model on 26 OECD countries of figure
{{< var p.fig_US_OECDdata >}} in one main variant: every country keeps its own workers per retiree, income
distribution and observed design, and takes from the U.S. the cost of redistribution as the elasticity
$\varepsilon$, so that it faces $\lambda_i = \varepsilon\,\Pi_i/R_i$ at its own ratio of the pay-as-you-go return
to the market return, the discount factor $\beta$ and the propensities to vote by income group. The test holds
these, the preferences and, in layer 1, the political weight of the old $\omega$ common to all countries (layer 2
calibrates each country's $\omega$ to its pension spending), and the sections below relax them one at a time and then
extend the sample to every country of the figure.

## The paper's variant {#esc-oecd26-paper}

The paper reports this variant in figure {{< var p.fig_OECD26_layer1 >}} and table
{{< var p.table_OECD26_slopes >}}, and each country's political weight and design in table
{{< var p.table_OECD26_omega >}}. Spending falls with population growth in the data and in layer 1 (layer 2 matches
spending by construction); spending rises with the Bismarckian index and the index falls with population growth in
the data and in both layers; and the index falls with the Gini in both layers, significantly in layer 1 only, where
the data show a rise that is not significant. The variants below are read against these signs.

## The U.S. λ in every country {#esc-oecd26-size}

Every country takes the U.S. cost parameter $\lambda$ itself in place of $\varepsilon$, so that its cost does not move
with its ratio $\Pi/R$, and the U.S. anchor is recalibrated under it; at the U.S. ratio the two are the same cost.
The ratio falls as a population ages, so a country whose ratio is below the U.S. one, as most are, faces a larger cost
under $\lambda$ than under $\varepsilon$, and each of them chooses a more Bismarckian design, as the UK and France do in
the deep test of section {{< var p.sec_esc_deepTest >}}. The index then falls more steeply with population growth in
both layers, and spending rises a little less steeply with the index; the index's relation with the Gini keeps its
sign and its significance, or its absence, in each layer.

## Each country's return at the U.S. one {#esc-oecd26-beta}

Setting each country's $\beta$ so that its return in 2020 is the U.S. one, in place of the U.S. $\beta$ itself, has
no exhibit here: table {{< var p.table_OECD26_robustness >}} in appendix {{< var p.app_oecd26 >}} of the paper
reports its slopes under both costs and at both sources of the propensities to vote.

## Each country's own turnout {#esc-oecd26-turnout}

Each country's propensities to vote by income group now come from the CSES. The U.S. anchor is recalibrated at its
own CSES profile, which raises $\varepsilon$, and Luxembourg, with no CSES election, leaves data and model alike. The
relations the test reproduces at the U.S. turnout keep their signs: spending falls with population growth, about as
steeply in layer 1 as in the data on these countries, and rises with the index in both layers, and the index falls
with population growth in both layers. On the Gini, where the data show no significant relation, layer 1's slope of
the index nearly vanishes and layer 2's takes the data's sign, neither significantly, while layer 1's slope of
spending keeps the sign opposite to the data's. In layer 2 the UK, which the paper's variant places above the U.S.
design, falls below it, on the side where the deep test of section {{< var p.sec_esc_deepTest >}} places it, and
France's design moves toward the one the deep test gives it (table {{< var x.OECD26_Omega_cses >}}).

## All the countries {#esc-oecd26-all}

Korea, Mexico and Turkey join the sample, at the paper's variant. The data's slope of spending on the Gini then
turns negative, the model's sign, and the data's slope of the index on population growth flattens toward layer 1's.
The other signs are those on the paper's sample: spending falls with population growth and rises with the index in
the data and in the model, the model's spending rising more steeply with the index; the index falls with population
growth in the data and in both layers; and the index rises with the Gini in the data, not significantly, where it
falls in both layers, significantly in layer 1 only. The table after the slopes gives the political weight of the old
each country's spending implies.
